title: The Surangama Sutra (Class Part 6)
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of recognizing and transcending the ego and its attachments in Buddhist practice, rather than becoming overly identified with spiritual experiences or states. This includes being aware of the "demonic" tendencies that can arise from advanced practice, which are not external entities but rather manifestations of one's own nature. By cultivating a clear understanding of reality and letting go of attachment to specific states or identities, practitioners can move beyond ego-based limitations and achieve true liberation.

sentences.text: *[Kanho Chris Burkhart and IkuShun Desiree Webster share this talk.
Speaker labels mark the handovers the recording makes clear.
In some stretches the recording does not show which of them is speaking, so those passages carry no new label.]*
**IkuShun Desiree Webster:** So thanks for joining us for this very last one.
I'm going to talk about that last major part of the book describing the demonic states that can arise from advanced practice.
I don't know how many of you are following along in the text, but it sounds worse than it is.
I actually really enjoyed this part.
It was really interesting to me.
So anyway, we're going to talk about that.

It says that they occur when the practitioner is breaking his or her attachments to the five aggregates, when there is still the presence of ego, which really, all these states to me feel like just different ego states.
And it says in there that they don't occur to people that aren't in these advanced states.
But there were a few things in there that were really interesting, so we'll stop when we come to those.
I felt like it was ego, when everything is still me, mine.
And just like when Mara comes to the Buddha at his awakening, and tried all these different things to tempt him and to change his mind and everything, I felt like it was like that.
So in the intro, again, it's noted that these also occur under the influence of spiritual charlatans and their cults.
That's a general thread through the book, which I found interesting.
The demonic states are described with examples concerning each of the five Skandhas, and we'll just have a little sample of each of those.
But the commentator says something in the beginning that I thought was really important.
*He says fifty demonic states are described in the section.
And in fact, there are countless numbers of these states.
And the demonic states are basically nothing but a mass of yin energy, which come from our yin thoughts.*
So I'm taking it that those are the scattered, delusional kind of energy.
*They include thoughts of desire, anger and delusion.
They give rise to the aggregates of form, sense, perception, cognition, mental formations and consciousness, the five Skandhas.

And each of these aggregates, various kinds of yin energy naturally appear when your skill reaches a certain level.* It says if your skill hasn't reached that level, you won't encounter these demonic states, even if you want to.
And as we go through, at least the beginning ones, they didn't seem like demonic states to me at all, some of them.
Anyway, we'll talk about it.
*So he says, don't worry when they appear.
There's no need to fear being possessed by demons.
When these yin phenomena appear, you should remain calm, as if they didn't exist.
See them as not seeing them, hear them as not hearing them.
If you don't want to let your attention be diverted by sights, sounds, odors, flavors, objects of touch and objects of cognition, then the demonic states will have no way to harm you.
If you are without desire, anger and delusion, you subdue these states.
The demons you encounter in your practice are illusions produced from the yin thoughts and the yin energy in your own nature.*
So I think that's a big, important part of understanding: they're not coming from some other place.
They're not coming, I think, from spirits.
They're coming from your own nature.
*If you can remain unmoved by these illusory appearances, they will be no problem.
No matter what level you reach in your cultivation, do not become happy or afraid.* And that's the essence of what is needed to overcome the demonic states.
Again, I just think of the Buddha: first Mara tries this, then he tries this, then he tries all these ways of getting to him.
And he just remained calm and didn't buy into it.
And they went away.
So that feels like what Xuan Hua is saying too.

So now I'm going to start in each chapter in part 10 with an opening introduction paragraph from the Buddha, and then choose one or two of the examples in each section of the five aggregates, the five skandhas.
So chapter two, demonic states of mind associated with form.
*The Buddha says, you should know, Ananda, that when you sit in a place for awakening, all your thoughts may melt away.
When your thoughts come to a halt, only the essential awareness will remain.
Movement outside your mind will seem the same as stillness, and the presence of thoughts in your mind will seem the same as the absence of thoughts.*
*When you abide in this state, having entered samadhi, you will be like someone who ordinarily can see clearly but finds himself in a dark place.
His essential nature will be wonderfully pure, but his mind does not yet emit light.
He is in the region of the aggregate of forms.
When his mind's vision does become bright, then* the ten directions *will open up before him and the darkness will be dispelled.
Having come to the end of the aggregate of forms, he will now transcend the turbidity of time.
His contemplations showed him that illusion of solid matter is a basis of this aggregate.*

So the first thing that could happen, he says: *Ananda, in the midst of his mental darkness, this person's intense scrutiny within his wondrous awareness may reveal that the four primary elements are not ultimately interwoven in the body.
Then in an instant, he will be able to leave his body.
This state is called the essential awareness, being able to emerge into one's surroundings.
What the practitioner has gained is temporary.
It does not indicate that he has become a sage.
There is nothing unwholesome about his state unless he thinks he is now a sage.
If he does think he is now a sage, he will be open to a host of deviant influences.*
So this pattern of what he's saying is interwoven in all of these fifty states: about not thinking that he's a sage.
That's where people get caught in things.
So further, this was the fourth one in this section.
*Further, in the midst of his mental darkness, a brilliant light may appear within this person's mind.
And then shine forth to imbue everything through the ten directions with a purple golden color of the river Jambu.
He may see creatures of every kind becoming the thus come ones.

At this moment, he will see Virochana Buddha sitting upon a* dais *of celestial light and surrounded by a thousand Buddhas while seated on a lotus flower will appear in a hundred million lands at once.
This state is called the mind illuminates all worlds clearly and in detail.
There is nothing unwholesome about this stage unless he thinks that he's now a sage.
If he thinks he's a sage, he'll be open to deviant influences.*
I like these couple of sections in here because it just reminds me of interconnection and Indra's net, that whole thing.
It doesn't feel like any demonic stage.
It feels like, oh, kind of seeing the nature of things in the way of interconnectedness.
So this next one's really interesting.
It's chapter three, ten demonic states of mind associated with the aggregate of sense perception.
*Ananda, as this good person practices Samadhi and as her mind becomes still, she will no longer experience the aggregate of form.
She may see the mind of Buddhas appear to her as a mirror, but she may not know how to use this mind.
She may undergo what seems to her to be a kind of paralysis.*
*It is as if a deviant being has come into contact with her mind and has prevented moving.
Even though her hands and feet are intact and her vision and hearing are unimpaired, she's now in the region of the aggregate of the sense perception.
If the paralysis continues, subsides, her mind will be able to leave her body and she will be able to look back and see her own face.
She will be able to stay or go as she pleases without further hindrance.
Having reached the end of the aggregate of sense perception, she will now transcend the turbidity of perception.
She now contemplates how this aggregate arises and she sees that its basis lies in illusion and deluded thinking.*
*Ananda, in this situation, this good person experiences an inner light of brilliance.
If she has been restraining her mind too severely, then wherever she sees beings illuminated by the light that shines forth from her mind, she may immediately be overwhelmed by a boundless sorrow.
She will look upon even mosquitoes and worms as she would look upon a newborn child.
Her mind will be filled with pity and she will frequently burst into tears without knowing why.
This state is called an excess of severity in one's own practice.*
Well, I read this and I thought, oh my gosh, that's me.
I've done that, and it was so weird for me to read that.
It's not that I think I'm in any stage or anything.
But it was also interesting to see that it says the state is called an excess of severity in one's practice.
Even when I was four years old, I squished a mosquito by mistake and I went screaming and crying into the house and telling my mom and dad.
Anyway, in some ways I'm too sensitive, I'm too much in that realm.
So I read it and thought, oh my gosh, that's me.
*This state is called an excess of severity in one's practice.
If she understands this state, she will not suppose that she has become a sage and will not be confused.
Eventually, the state will disappear of its own accord.
But if she thinks she's a sage, then a demonic sorrow will enter into the depths of her mind.
Whenever she sees someone, she will feel such sadness that she will break into uncontrollable sobs.
Having lost the ability to enter correct Samadhi, she is certain to fall.* Luckily, it's not that.
So, yeah.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Can I just add something to this?
Yeah.
When we read something like this, it's interesting to see how it relates to us and our own experience.
Like Desiree, I had this time where I would just sit in sesshin and bawl, without being sad or anything specific.
But it's laced into this common ground that we all share, these experiences, whether we talk about them or not.
And some people have these grandiose experiences and others have these tiny little ones.
Passages like this in the Surangama let us feel into this and see that it's not just Red Cedar and it's Chan Buddhism in China a thousand years ago.
I get this feeling of tangling through the lineage into the past and by doing that also, of course, into the future.
There will be people in the future and they will struggle with exactly the same things we fight with and have the same experiences.
That is one way of looking at this.
If you plan on studying the Surangama in the future, because I certainly will: we are not done with each other yet.
**IkuShun Desiree Webster:** Yeah, yeah, thanks.
It's such a, gosh, I don't know how to say it, intricate and full of these things that I really struggled with.
But I find that it has been very beneficial in this way, that it really shines a light on some of these areas in myself.
But yeah, anyway, I think it takes a lot longer than our six week survey class to really get into it.
But it's like a taste of it.
All right, so chapter four was the ten demonic stages of mind associated with the aggregate of cognition.

*Ananda, when a good person who has been practicing Samadhi no longer experiences the aggregate of sense perception, he will be able to leave his body as if he were a bird escaping from a cage, although he will not have put an end to his outflows.
He retains his ordinary body, but he already has the potential to ascend through the sixty stages of the Bodhisattva.*
*He is now able to use his mind to create a spiritual body that can travel about freely just as he wishes.
He will be like a man who talks while sound asleep, but does not realize he's doing it.
His voice will be clear enough and his words will make sense enough to be understood by others who are awake.
He's now in the region of aggregate of cognition.*
So this one also reminded me of something.
There's a very famous Chinese teacher, Lin Chi, who's in the Rinzai lineage, and there's a book by Thich Nhat Hanh about Lin Chi.
In it he's talking about how you will be able to go to all of these distant worlds and things while still being in your armchair.
That reminds me of what this is saying: this freedom of moving around.
*So now if the movement of thought in his mind ceases such that all superfluous cognition dissipates, then his awakened mind will cease to be defiled.
He will understand with complete clarity the deaths and rebirths of the classes of being without exception.
He has reached the end of the aggregate of cognition and will now be able to transcend the turbidity of affliction.
He will contemplate how this aggregate arises and you will see that its basis is the pervasive influence of* deluded *mental activity.*

So the first one: *Ananda,* [unclear: "in the wonder of that, in the wonder of that"] *ensues when a good person no longer experiences the aggregate of sense perception, she will not give rise to any harmful anxiety.
As she perfects her concentration, she will experience light and within her Samadhi she may come to crave a more ample illumination.
She will intensify her concentrated thought as she seeks avidly to develop her skill.
Then a celestial demon seizing the opportunity it has been waiting for will descend upon some other person and possess her.
This other person will not realize that she's been possessed.
And so when she is speaking about the sutras, will claim that she herself has entered the supreme nirvana.
She will seek out the good person who has avidly desired to develop her skill.*
And this is a really lengthy discussion section about people being possessed and you not knowing.
Again, it's the charlatan kind of thing.
But the commentary says: *if you encounter people who are manifesting spiritual powers as described in this passage, don't get carried away by what you see, no matter what it is.
Rather look on at the situation as it exists, neither elated or disgusted.
Then if you want to determine whether someone is genuine or phony, whether he is a bodhisattva or a demon, you can look at the following two things.
First, see if he has any sexual desires,* I would guess inappropriate.
*And second, see if he is greedy for money.
If he cheats people in order to satisfy his lust or avarice, then he is not genuine.*
The other thing about reading all these passages is understanding how we're all living with these delusive desires, no matter what they are.
So whether I see them as possessed or not, it's just their own mind that is possessing them in terms of greed, hatred and ignorance.
So yeah, people are around.
Chapter five, ten demonic states of mind associated with the aggregates of mental formations.
*So, Ananda, when a good person who has been practicing Samadhi has reached the end of the aggregate of cognition, the usual cognitive processes involved in dreaming will disappear from her mind.
For her, there will be no longer any difference between waking and sleeping.
Her awareness will be luminous as empty and still as a cloudless sky.

She will view all the phenomena in the world, the mountains, the rivers and everything else as mere reflections that briefly appear in a clear mirror, leaving nothing behind, disappearing without a trace, receiving and reflecting nothing more.
She has done away with habitual and long cherished karmic impressions.
Only the true essence of consciousness remains.
As the source of coming into being and ceasing to be as exposed to her, she may have a clear vision, which extends throughout the ten directions of all the kinds of beings in their 12 classes.
Although she cannot yet discern the thread of causes that is unique to each individual life, she will be able to perceive the origin that is common to all lives.
This origin will appear to her as a subtle, glimmering, vibrating mirage.*
*This is the ultimate point, the pivotal point, at which the faculties and their objects meet.
She has reached the region of the aggregate of mental formations.

If she is able to see the subtle, glimmering vibrations, which are the origin of beings, revert to that clarity that is their original nature, then her habitual karma will become still, just as clear waters become calm when waves are still.
She will have reached the end of the aggregate of mental formations.
She will be able to transcend the turbidity of individual beings.
She will contemplate how this aggregate arises, and she will see that its basis lies in mental distortions and the deep recesses of our mind.*

And from the footnotes, the paragraphs following, which I won't read, describe practitioners who run into difficulty with errors that involve wrong views, which we're going to talk about in a little bit.
I thought I had something, but I forget now, so maybe I'll remember.
So, chapter six is demonic.
Oh, I know what I was going to say: last week, Chris talked, she gave that demonstration about the knots, with a scarf.
I think he talks later, but it's this idea that you can't untie the bottom knot before you untie all of them; they come in a progression.
So that's what is happening here.
He's talking about these stages of letting go, and you can't pull one out of the middle.
It's like this progression of development.
So, chapter six is the demonic stages of mind associated with the aggregate of consciousness.

*In this chapter on the last of the five aggregates, the Buddha explains that there are still many ways in which the practitioner can find themselves off the path, such as concluding that one has fully achieved one's goal or concluding that one has a special ability and believing that one has succeeded in exercising it.
Or, making suppositions about a void drawing conclusions concerning that void.*

And I think it's in Genjokoan where Dogen talks [unclear: "like Warren's"] about people that think that they're totally enlightened are deluded and people that are totally enlightened don't think that they're enlightened.
So it's easy to get stuck, I think, in these places where maybe after an experience we think, "Oh my gosh, I've got it."
*So however, once you have come to the end of the aggregate of consciousness, your faculties will function interchangeably.
And then on the basis of that mutual functioning, you will be able to reach the bodhisattvas level of Vajra-like wisdom.
When you experience the full illumination of that refined state of mind, you will undergo transformation.
Your mind will become resplendent, like a moon enclosed in pure crystal, and then you will leap over all the stages of the bodhisattvas path.
The ten stages of stabilizing mind, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the four additional practices,*
which we talked about last week, all of those, the ten dedications, the ten practices are also present in many pages in the Avatamsaka.
So that also seems to be like this kind of stage of developing the bodhisattva ideal.
*So these practices, the Vajra-like ten grounds and the equivalent enlightenment in which everything understanding is finally perfected.
You will enter into the wondrous and magnificent multitude of the thus come ones, vast as the sea, you will attain the perfection of full awakening, in which there is nothing that is attained.

All the Buddha's world-honored ones of the past, while calmly abiding in shamatha and while practicing contemplative insight, their enlightened understanding, they analyze these subtle demonic activities.
Once you can clearly recognize these demonic states when they occur, you will be able to cleanse your mind of those defilements and you will not fall prey to the wrong views.
Then the demonic states associated with the aggregates will be eradicated and the celestial demons will be utterly defeated.*
So it was strange to me when I was reading this last fifty demonic states of mind that it's actually really encouraging, I think, more so than a lot of the book.
It's like this encouragement and also this beautiful...
I enjoyed this last section.
So chapter seven, it's entitled the five aggregates arise from delusion, and it's just kind of a recap.
*The five aggregates in Ananda are simply the development of these five kinds of deluded mental activity.
Now you also wish to know what the defining attributes of each of the aggregates are and how coarsely refined they are.
Form and emptiness aggregates are the defining attributes of an aggregate of form.
Contact and separation are the defining attributes of an aggregate of sense perception.
What is recorded and what is not recorded are the defining attributes of the aggregate of cognition.
Coming into being and perishing are the defining attributes of the aggregate of mental formations.
Entering into the state of deep clarity and being stored in that deep clarity are the defining attributes of the aggregate of consciousness.
These five aggregates arise in successive layers beginning with the coming into being of consciousness.
Their perishing begins with the ceasing to be a form.
You may suddenly reach an understanding of the principle of the aggregates.
And on that basis, you may presume the aggregates will vanish altogether.
But in fact, they do not vanish at once.
They must be ended in sequence,* which is what I was talking about with the knots.
So there's one other little section, chapter eight, the merit of teaching the sharing Dharma, entitled.
Yeah, that's what it's entitled.
And I'm not going to read that.
But I just wanted to say that many of these great sutras, the Diamond Sutra, Avatam, the Lotus, they all end with the merit of reading their particular sutra.
So with that, we come to the conclusion of the sharing Dharma Sutra.

I have a little bit here for us for a group discussion in a little bit, but we'll let Chris give us the final final statement about the sharing Dharma, and then we'll take a break and then we'll come back and just have a little bit of a discussion.
And it's a really small group, so that should work good.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** It's not even that much that I want to say.
I was practicing the sutra for about nine months altogether.
One of the key elements for me was that the sutra asked me directly how my sense input and also my sense desire influence how I perceive the world around me, how I deal with it.
It's really clear that the world says, well, if you have great attachments to, I'm just going to say good food, taste, that's a pretty harmless one.
It's not just that I have this specific sense desire towards taste.
It's also that now I have this external driver that's only important because it's in my mind.
Because then the mind reaches out and says, "Oh, I want something tasty.
This isn't quite it.
I want this and that."
And so it can be quite distracting.
If we apply that to every area of our life, it shows these entanglements, how they can yank us around.
Some people have almost crazy desire for certain possessions, like always a used car, or to have a big house or status or whatever.
And the second thing I found remarkable about the Shurangama is it mentally takes me through all the hoops of the six of the skandhas.
So form, sensation, vision, hearing, and so on.
It really was an intellectual exercise.
But how does this interplay from sense input and the aggregates?
Who's in the driver's seat?
Is it the elements, I want to observe taste or touch?
Or is it my desires that want to go out and grab these things?
There was a passage, I think it was last week, where we read how the different senses go out and want to grab their own goodies.
The ears want to have something nice to listen to and the taste buds want something interesting.
So even if I don't directly connect with those concepts, the intellectual engagement with the concept itself can somewhat loosen that bondage a little bit.

If I have this crazy desire for a cookie, which I have a lot, to understand that it's just this desire, and that it's only hanging in there for such a long time because I continually hit the refresh button.
If I didn't pay any attention to my desire, it would go away pretty quick.
However, by having the desire influence the strength of that wanting, it can get pretty big and lead people to pretty silly mistakes.
And last, not least, if we really look at our bodies and our minds, we can clearly see how little of it is ours.
Actually, nothing is really ours, but we'd like to think that something has to be mine.
But it's really helpful every once in a while to dive deep into where this body is coming from and who has sacrificed to keep me alive for these 67 years.
So I would encourage you to pursue those ideas, maybe in the form of the Shurangama Sutra, which, like Desiree said, was a bit more difficult than we had originally thought.
But the longer I hang with it, the more it's starting to give back.
And also, if you think the Shurangama is not a book to be put aside lightly, but to be tossed with great force, I get that too, but have patience with the book and it'll kind of turn a bit.
**IkuShun Desiree Webster:** Thanks, Chris.

I was just thinking that I might talk a little bit about what our discussion is going to be before we take a break, so that maybe you have a chance to think about it a little bit and come back, think about what Chris said, and think about this little paragraph that I'm going to read.
Then we'll take a break and then we'll come back and have a little discussion.
I don't know, seems like I skipped something.
But:

*In the third concern in the introduction, addressed by the Buddhist teachings is the need for proper understanding of the difference between one's true mind and one's distinction making consciousness, since understanding is a prerequisite for right practice.*
So for me, a lot of the book, the feeling of it, the focus, the thread was for us to see how our delusive mind really takes us away from right view.
We're running around all the time with totally delusive ideas about things, and they sort of carry us away from that.
So I think that right view is a really strong thread throughout the teachings of the Shurangama.

It's been in the forefront of my mind as we journey along, especially in this last section of the book, because without right view, no matter how much we practice, we're going to be heading down the wrong path.
And one of my favorite things that Chris has ever said in a talk: we're going to go into the brambles.
So thinking about that, maybe we can open up a discussion after the break and talk about this last section or really any of the sections of the Sutra in regards to right view.
What are some of the ways that the Sutra tries to help us cultivate right view?
What are some examples from your life that you've been able to remember to help you cut through delusive thinking?
I'd like to spend time on that, and I have a couple helpful hints.
So we can think about: did this action come from me, myself, mine?
And did it come from the idea that I have a separate self or my ego?
One of the things that Chris talked about, oh my gosh, a part of it that's good for me, but really hard to see, is that it really showed me all of my habit energies.
I just have millions of habit energies, and just really working with those, looking at them like wanting the cookies or whatever, there's just an endless amount of them.
But when we think about right view, we're wanting to hold that deeper sense of ourselves that's beyond a separate self, beyond the thinking, beyond thinking that we're permanent, whatever.
So anyway, I just want to thank everybody for hanging in there with us, with the Shungama.
It was definitely a challenging sutra, but like Chris says, I have to admit that it's sinking in a little bit more.
I've been like this with it, where some days I was just like, "What did you say?"
Heave it with force and then other times, pieces, I'm like, "Oh yeah."
So anyway, let's take a break for five minutes and then come back and just have a little discussion.
